title: K-D-Sh
hook: kadosh, kiddush, kiddushin (marriage): all mean set apart

segments.voice: Yesterday, B-R-K: blessing, knee and pool, and the week looked back on. Your line was blessing bends. Did you bend down for anything with thanks? A new week, and a new root. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-nine.

Under a wedding canopy, a groom holds out a plain ring. The bride offers her finger, and in front of witnesses he says one short sentence in Hebrew. The word at its heart is mekudeshet. Now go a long way back, to the desert, where Moses is given plans for a tent of woven curtains and gold, with one line of purpose. In the King James words: "let them make me a sanctuary; that I may dwell among them." The Hebrew for sanctuary there is mikdash. A ring and a tent. They seem to belong to different worlds. Underneath, they share one root: kuf, dalet, shin. You met kuf on its own a couple of weeks ago. Today we dig up the whole root it begins.
screen: `A RING UNDER A CANOPY.` → `A TENT IN THE DESERT.` → `ONE ROOT: K-D-SH.`

segments.voice: K-D-Sh. Turn it four ways. First, the core. Kadosh, holy, from this root, means set apart: marked off from the ordinary, for something more. Second, a place. The mikdash, the sanctuary in the desert, is a space marked off from the camp around it. And notice what the verse gives as its reason. Not the gold, not the curtains, but a purpose: that I may dwell among them. The Temple in Jerusalem is remembered by the same word, the Beit HaMikdash, the house of the holy place. Third, a time. The Sabbath is a day set apart from the week, and on Friday night a cup of wine is lifted for kiddush, the words that mark where the week stops and the day of rest begins. The root does in time what the sanctuary does in space: it draws a border, and says this side is different. Fourth, a person. A Jewish marriage begins with kiddushin. In the traditional words, the groom tells the bride that with this ring she is mekudeshet to him: set apart for him. One person, chosen out of all others, and the choosing itself is what makes the bond holy. Place, time, person. In this root, holiness isn't floating somewhere above life. It's made by marking a line around something and keeping it. Set apart doesn't mean locked away. It means given a place of its own.
screen: `KADOSH: HOLY, SET APART.` · `MIKDASH: A PLACE SET APART.` · `KIDDUSH: A DAY SET APART.` · `KIDDUSHIN: A PERSON SET APART.` · then, large: `SET APART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set one thing apart. Settle, and breathe. Look around you, or think through your day ahead. Choose one thing to mark off from the rest. A cup you'll drink from slowly. Ten minutes with your phone in another room. A meal eaten without hurry. A conversation you'll give your whole attention. Decide on it now. Then sit, and notice the difference between that one thing and everything around it, the line you've just drawn. If you pray, you can ask that this one thing be set apart. The bell holds the time.
K-D-Sh. Kuf, dalet, shin: the root of kadosh, holy; mikdash, the sanctuary; kiddush, over the wine; and kiddushin, marriage. All set apart. Today's word.
Your line: set apart. Today, keep the one thing you chose, and don't let the rest of the day spill into it. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: On Friday evening, Jewish families say kiddush over wine to set the Sabbath apart; a Jewish wedding begins with kiddushin, when the groom gives the bride a ring with a formula saying she is set apart for him; the sanctuary in Exodus, and later the Temple, is called by the same root: mikdash.

pairs: a sanctuary, a place set apart
said over wine for the Sabbath
the start of a Jewish marriage

myth: the Hebrew word for sanctuary, mikdash, shares a root with kadosh
kuf, dalet, shin: a place set apart.
kiddush and kiddushin come from the same root as kadosh
in this root, holy means locked away from ordinary life
it means marked off, given a place of its own: a place, a day, a person.

fork.setup: under the wedding canopy, the groom gives the ring and says the bride is mekudeshet to him. what does that root say she is?
fork.reveal: set apart. mekudeshet grows from k-d-sh, the root of kadosh, holy: one person, chosen out of all others.

original.note: Hebrew: a sanctuary, a place set apart, from the root kuf, dalet, shin.

trapdoor: what you thought: a wedding ring, a desert tent and a Friday-night cup have nothing in common.
what it means: all three grow from k-d-sh: a person, a place and a time, each set apart.
what a scholar hears: the mikdash of Exodus 25:8, the Friday-night kiddush and the groom's mekudeshet share one root.

notes: Exodus 25:8 fragment quoted as KJV (1769); confirm exact wording and punctuation. Mikdash is the Hebrew there.
Genesis 2:3 kept as background for the Sabbath being a day set apart (paraphrased, not quoted).
Betrothal formula (harei at mekudeshet li) paraphrased; the formula is said by the groom. 'In front of witnesses' given without a number.
'The Temple in Jerusalem is remembered by the same word, the Beit HaMikdash': standard name; confirm.
Hook callback 'you met kuf a couple of weeks ago' refers to day 1347.

Editor pass: day 1347 (Kuf) already taught Leviticus 19:2, Isaiah 6:3 with the Kedushah, Genesis 2:3 and kiddush, and the original word kadosh. This day was rebuilt to avoid repeating it: the hook is now a wedding ring and the desert sanctuary (Exodus 25:8, mikdash) instead of the Friday cup (also used in 1355's hook) and the Kedushah; the teach turns place, time and person; Leviticus, Isaiah and the quoted Genesis 2:3 cut; match, myth, fork, original (now mikdash) and trapdoor rewritten to match.
